abstract: By decomposing the image formation process into a sequential application of denoising autoencoders, diffusion models (DMs) achieve state-of-the-art synthesis results on image data and beyond. Additionally, their formulation allows for a guiding mechanism to control the image generation process without retraining. However, since these models typically operate directly in pixel space, optimization of powerful DMs often consumes hundreds of GPU days and inference is expensive due to sequential evaluations. To enable DM training on limited computational resources while retaining their quality and flexibility, we apply them in the latent space of powerful pretrained autoencoders. In contrast to previous work, training diffusion models on such a representation allows for the first time to reach a near-optimal point between complexity reduction and detail preservation, greatly boosting visual fidelity. By introducing cross-attention layers into the model architecture, we turn diffusion models into powerful and flexible generators for general conditioning inputs such as text or bounding boxes and high-resolution synthesis becomes possible in a convolutional manner. Our latent diffusion models (LDMs) achieve new state-of-the-art scores for image inpainting and class-conditional image synthesis and highly competitive performance on various tasks, including text-to-image synthesis, unconditional image generation and super-resolution, while significantly reducing computational requirements compared to pixel-based DMs.

sections.body: The introduction states that training the most powerful diffusion models can take hundreds of GPU days, with one cited case at 150 to 1000 V100 days, and that producing 50k samples takes approximately 5 days on a single A100 GPU. The authors propose training diffusion models in the latent space of pretrained autoencoders, so the autoencoder handles perceptual compression. The listed contributions are reconstructions that preserve more detail than prior work, competitive results on several tasks at lower cost, cross-attention conditioning for text and layouts, convolutional sampling of images up to about 1024×1024 px, and released pretrained models.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Pixel-space diffusion models are costly to train and sample, so the paper moves them into a learned latent space.

sections.body: The related work section says GANs give good samples but are hard to optimize and struggle to capture the full data distribution. Likelihood-based methods are better behaved to optimize but spend capacity on imperceptible high-frequency detail. Autoregressive models are limited to low resolution by computational demands and sequential sampling. Two-stage approaches model compressed latent spaces, but the high compression needed for feasible training limits quality, while less compression is costly. Diffusion models reach top results, yet pixel-space evaluation makes them slow to sample and expensive to train. The authors propose latent diffusion models that scale more gently to higher dimensional latent spaces.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier generative approaches trade off sample quality, speed and resolution, and pixel-space diffusion models are costly to optimize and sample.

sections.body: An encoder E maps an image to a latent with downsampling factor f = H/h, and a decoder D reconstructs the image. The autoencoder combines a perceptual loss with a patch-based adversarial objective. Two regularizations are compared: KL-reg., a slight KL penalty toward a standard normal, and VQ-reg., a vector quantization layer inside the decoder. A diffusion model is then trained on the latents with a time-conditional UNet built mainly from 2D convolutional layers. For conditioning, an encoder `tau_theta` projects inputs such as text, and cross-attention maps them into intermediate UNet layers. The section states that this design allows mild compression while keeping image detail.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Latent diffusion models train a UNet on latents from a perceptual autoencoder, and add cross-attention for conditioning inputs such as text.

sections.body: The experiments vary the downsampling factor from 1 to 32 on a single A100 with a fixed budget. On ImageNet over 2M training steps, LDM-1 and LDM-2 train slowly, while LDM-32 limits sample quality, so LDM-4 to LDM-16 offer the best balance. Results include a new FID of 5.11 on CelebA-HQ for unconditional generation, a 1.45B parameter text-to-image model evaluated on MS-COCO, and class-conditional ImageNet results that outperform ADM with lower compute. For inpainting, the authors report a speed-up of at least 2.7× over pixel-based LDM-1 and an FID improvement of at least 1.6×. The super-resolution results are described as competitive, with LDM-SR outperforming SR3 in FID.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Latent models with downsampling factors 4 to 8 reach much lower Fréchet inception distance (FID) than pixel-based diffusion, a gap of 38 after 2M steps.

sections.body: The limitations section states that sequential sampling remains slower than GANs. It also says autoencoder reconstruction can become a bottleneck for tasks that need fine-grained accuracy in pixel space, and the authors assume their super-resolution models are somewhat limited in this respect. The societal impact section notes that lower training and inference costs could widen access, but also that image generation can ease the creation of deep fakes and misinformation. It raises concern about generative models revealing sensitive training data, and says that the extent to which diffusion models do so is not yet fully understood. It also notes that the models can reproduce or amplify dataset biases.
sections.heading: Limitations & Societal Impact
sections.headline: Latent models still sample more slowly than GANs, and autoencoder reconstruction can limit tasks that need fine pixel accuracy.

sections.body: The conclusion describes latent diffusion models as a simple and efficient way to significantly improve the training and sampling efficiency of denoising diffusion models without degrading their quality. It states that, together with the cross-attention conditioning mechanism, the experiments showed favorable results compared to prior leading methods across a wide range of conditional image synthesis tasks. It emphasizes that these results were obtained without task-specific architectures.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The authors conclude that latent diffusion improves training and sampling efficiency without degrading quality across several conditional tasks.

sections.body: The changelog lists a retrained 1.45B parameter text-to-image model, an updated class-conditional ImageNet model with larger batch size, and a user study for inpainting and super-resolution. The derivation section explains the signal-to-noise formulation and the reweighted denoising objective. The guidance section describes post-hoc image guiding with a Gaussian guider and an LPIPS variant. Further sections give layout-to-image results, computational requirements converted from A100 days to V100 days with an assumed ×2.2 speedup, and the adversarial and regularization objectives for the autoencoders.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers the changelog, the diffusion objective derivation, guidance, extra results, compute comparisons and autoencoder training details.
